title: Companies Act, 2013 — Section 113 (Representation of corporations at meeting of companies and of creditors)

content.overview: Section 113(1) allows a body corporate (whether a company under the Act or not) to authorise a person by resolution of its Board of Directors or other governing body to act as its representative: (a) if it is a member, at any meeting of the company or of any class of members; (b) if it is a creditor (including a debenture-holder), at any meeting of creditors held under the Act, rules, or a debenture or trust deed. Section 113(2) entitles the authorised person to exercise the same rights and powers, including voting by proxy and postal ballot, on behalf of the body corporate as that body could exercise if it were an individual member, creditor or debenture-holder.
content.glance: A body corporate that is a member or creditor may, by board or governing-body resolution, authorise a person to represent it at the relevant meeting with the same rights (including proxy and postal ballot) as if it were an individual.
content.study:
## Section 113 — representation of corporations

**Subsection (1): authorisation.** A body corporate, whether a company within the meaning of this Act or not, may—
- (a) if it is a member of a company within the meaning of this Act, by resolution of its Board of Directors or other governing body, authorise such person as it thinks fit to act as its representative at any meeting of the company, or at any meeting of any class of members of the company;
- (b) if it is a creditor, including a holder of debentures, of a company within the meaning of this Act, by resolution of its directors or other governing body, authorise such person as it thinks fit to act as its representative at any meeting of any creditors of the company held in pursuance of this Act or of any rules made thereunder, or in pursuance of the provisions contained in any debenture or trust deed, as the case may be.

**Subsection (2): rights.** A person authorised under subsection (1) shall be entitled to exercise the same rights and powers, including the right to vote by proxy and by postal ballot, on behalf of the body corporate which he represents as that body could exercise if it were an individual member, creditor or holder of debentures of the company.

## Apply the provision
- Confirm that the entity is a body corporate (company under the Act or not) and is a member (clause (a)) or creditor/debenture-holder (clause (b)).
- Require a resolution of the Board or other governing body authorising the individual.
- The representative exercises the same rights as the body corporate would if it were an individual, including proxy and postal ballot.

Distinguish from section 112 (President/Governor). This note is a focused study aid; the topic remains under source and current-law review.

sections.heading: Subsection (1)(a): member body corporate
sections.body: A body corporate that is a member may, by board or governing-body resolution, authorise a person to act as its representative at any meeting of the company or of any class of members.

sections.heading: Subsection (1)(b): creditor body corporate
sections.body: A body corporate that is a creditor (including a debenture-holder) may, by resolution of its directors or other governing body, authorise a person to act as its representative at any creditors' meeting held under the Act, rules, or a debenture or trust deed.

sections.heading: Subsection (2): rights of the representative
sections.body: The authorised person may exercise the same rights and powers, including voting by proxy and postal ballot, as the body corporate could if it were an individual member, creditor or debenture-holder.

provisions.title: Companies Act, 2013 — Section 113 (Representation of corporations at meeting of companies and of creditors)

examples.title: Body corporate member authorises a representative
examples.body: A company that holds shares in another company passes a board resolution authorising an individual to act as its representative at the investee's AGM. Under section 113 that individual may exercise the same rights, including proxy and postal ballot, as the body corporate could if it were an individual member. This is an educational illustration.

examples.title: Debenture-holder body corporate at a creditors' meeting
examples.body: A body corporate holding debentures authorises a person by governing-body resolution to attend a creditors' meeting under a trust deed. Subsection (1)(b) and (2) apply. This is an educational illustration.

hypotheticals.question: Must the authorisation under section 113 be by board resolution, or can any officer appoint the representative?
hypotheticals.analysis: The statute requires a resolution of the Board of Directors or other governing body (clause (a)) or of its directors or other governing body (clause (b)). An informal appointment by an officer alone does not satisfy the section.

hypotheticals.question: Can the authorised representative vote by postal ballot?
hypotheticals.analysis: Yes. Subsection (2) expressly includes the right to vote by proxy and by postal ballot on behalf of the body corporate.

distinctions.title: Section 113 compared with section 112
distinctions.left: Section 113 — body corporate (member or creditor) authorises by board/governing-body resolution
distinctions.right: Section 112 — President or Governor as member appoints a representative

misconceptions.trap: Treating a partnership firm or unincorporated association as a body corporate under section 113.
misconceptions.correction: Section 113 applies to a body corporate (whether a company under the Act or not). Partnerships and unincorporated associations are not body corporates for this purpose.

misconceptions.trap: Assuming any letter of authority from a company officer is enough without a board or governing-body resolution.
misconceptions.correction: The statute requires a resolution of the Board of Directors or other governing body (or directors/governing body for creditors).

questionsAndAnswers.question: What does section 113 provide?
questionsAndAnswers.answer: A body corporate that is a member or a creditor (including a debenture-holder) may, by resolution of its Board or other governing body, authorise a person to act as its representative at the relevant company, class or creditors' meeting. That person may exercise the same rights and powers, including voting by proxy and postal ballot, as the body corporate could if it were an individual.
